definitions.definition: The observance and doctrine taught by Paśupati for the release of the paśus; also a follower of it. The Pāśupata Sūtra opens by announcing 'the Pāśupata rule of yoga'.
In the Purāṇas also the Vedic ash-vow of the Atharvaśiras ('pāśupata vrata'), distinguished by the Kūrma Purāṇa from the non-Vedic Pāśupata scriptures.
The Lord (Rudra, Maheśvara) as master of all bound souls; he 'reaches' and 'protects' them by infinite knowledge and lordship, and releases them by grace.
The Lord as possessor of unsurpassed powers of seeing and acting, eternally related to that lordship and not acquiring it (SDS ch. 6); he alone is not a paśu.

equivalents.note: the Pāśupata Pati is the independent efficient cause, not the Nyāya Īśvara who acts in dependence on karma

definitions.definition: Every conscious being other than the Lord - with body and organs (sāñjana) or without (nirañjana), including the gods from Brahmā down and those liberated by Sāṃkhya-Yoga - bound by the kalās; so called from 'seeing' (only the body) and 'being bound'.
Used in the same sense in the Śaiva sources that report on the Kāpālikas; no independent Kāpālika definition survives.

equivalents.note: both name the individual embodied soul; for the Pāśupata the paśu is eternal, pervasive and never becomes the Lord

definitions.definition: The bonds are the kalās called effects and instruments, by which the paśus are bound and made subject to sense-objects.

literal: the state of being a paśu

definitions.definition: Bondage: a beginningless lack of lordship (anaiśvarya) and dependence; its complete removal through connection with Maheśvara's lordship is the fifth purification.
The essence of bondage for Kauṇḍinya: the soul's lack of lordship, the obstruction of its powers; also listed by him as the fifth impurity.
The five categories that sum up the Pāśupata teaching: effect, cause, union, rule and the end of suffering; also the name of the system ('Pāñcārthika').
All that is dependent: vidyā, kalā and paśu - eternal, yet wholly subject to the Lord's will.
The Lord, who alone is independent and produces the effect at will, without depending on karma.
Śaṅkara: the Māheśvaras wrongly make Paśupati only the efficient cause; Brahman is both material and efficient cause.
The conjunction of the self with the Lord (through the mind); twofold - in action (muttering, meditation) and in the cessation of action.
Activity that produces merit: primary (the observance - vows and the six 'doors') and secondary (re-bathing and the like); it begins with ash, has censure in the middle and ends with feigned folly.
Liberation: twofold - the absolute cessation of all suffering, and the attainment of lordship consisting in the powers of knowing and acting; reached through the Lord's grace.
Yāmuna reports it as the absolute cessation of pain understood as the destruction of the soul's special qualities (opponent's report).

equivalents.note: the Pāśupata name for liberation; it adds the Lord's powers to cessation
Nyāya's apavarga is cessation only; the Pāśupatas insist theirs is more (SDS 6/3)

definitions.definition: A quality of the paśu, part of the effect: either cognitive (discriminating or not) or non-cognitive (merit and demerit).
The insentient part of the effect, dependent on the sentient: ten 'effects' (five elements, five qualities) and thirteen 'instruments' (ten senses, buddhi, ahaṃkāra, manas); they are the bonds.
A paśu joined to body and organs; its opposite, nirañjana, is a paśu without them.
The Lord's nature and motive: in play he produces, favours and conceals the threefold effect; 'deva' is derived from div 'to play'.

equivalents.note: both name divine activity as play, without need

definitions.definition: The Lord's quality of willing: because he wills, he produces the effects at once or in sequence as he wishes and does not depend on karma.
The Lord's grace (īśaprasāda), by which alone the end of suffering is reached; also listed as the fifth means. As 'clarity of mind' (mateḥ prasāda) it is one of the strengths.
The Lord's favouring of the effect; also the teacher's right favour to qualified disciples, which preserves the tradition and itself leads to the end of suffering.
Three: perception (sensory and of the self), inference (as-before, from-the-remainder, seen-in-general), and scripture.
The teaching that has come down through the succession of teachers from Maheśvara.
The Lord of the Pāśupata Sūtra, near whom the liberated brahmin does not return and with whom he attains union; gods and ancestors are both in him.
The Lord whose southern image is worshipped and whose troops the perfected yogin leads; source of the scriptural tradition.
Epithet of Śiva as 'maker of all happiness and nirvāṇa'; devotion is to be to none but Śaṅkara.
The Lord as 'Īśāna of all knowledges, lord of all beings', invoked in the fifth brahma-mantra that closes the Sūtra.
Name of the Lord in the closing prayer 'may Śiva be mine, always Śiva'.
The deity of the Kālāmukha temples (e.g. Kedāreśvara at Balligāve).
Direct conjunction with Rudra, attained by the ascetic dwelling in the cremation ground.
The final and certain attainment of Rudra's proximity, from which no one returns.
The perfected yogin endowed with the powers, chief among Mahādeva's troops (Nandin, Mahākāla and the rest).

notes: Distinct from the Gāṇapatya deity Mahāgaṇapati.

definitions.definition: The fifth gain; also the marks of perfection of the yogin (not subject to others, invulnerable, unaging, unobstructed etc.).
The liberated's power of knowing: seeing, hearing, thinking, knowing (all treatises) and omniscience.

equivalents.note: Kauṇḍinya calls the same power jñānaśakti (PABh 5.46)

definitions.definition: The liberated's power of acting: swiftness of mind, taking forms at will, and acting without organs.
The fifth mode of the power of seeing: knowledge of everything, said and unsaid, in brief and in detail.
The power of acting with unsurpassed speed.
The power to govern at will endless forms and instruments, independent of karma.
In the Mattavilāsa the Kāpālika claims that austerity gives the power to take any form (satire).

literal: the capacity of acting without organs

definitions.definition: Unsurpassed lordship even with the instruments withdrawn; Kauṇḍinya calls it the Pāśupata's distinction over others' isolation (kaivalya). The Sūtra lists 'vikaraṇa' and 'dharmitva' separately.
Of the self (bodily and mental), from beings and from the gods; also fivefold as womb, birth, ignorance, old age and death.
The Pāśupata state: the initiate leaves the rules of his former āśrama and follows the restraints and observances of the state beyond the āśramas.
Name used by Śaiva scripture for the Pāśupata branch of the Atimārga.
The primary observance of ash-bathing, lying in ash, the sixfold offering, muttering and circumambulation.
The series of acts from ash-bathing to feigned folly; threefold as gift, worship and austerity; twofold as vows and doors; the second means to the gains.
The six feigned behaviours (snoring, trembling, limping, amorous gestures, senseless acts, senseless speech) that are 'doors' to the increase of merit and loss of demerit by producing dishonour.
The six-limbed offering: laughter, song, dance, the ḍuṇḍuṅ sound, prostration and muttering.
Loud laughter ('a-ha-ha', aṭṭahāsa) offered to the Lord; a vocal act.
Singing of the Lord's qualities, according to the rules of music; a vocal act of the offering.
Dance according to the dramaturgical rules, offered to the Lord; a bodily act.
A holy sound like a bull's bellow made by touching tongue-tip to palate; part of the offering.

notes: Also written huḍukkāra (SDS, Ratnaṭīkā) and dunduṃkāra (Sagar text).

definitions.definition: Homage to the Lord as part of the offering; for the Ratnaṭīkā a mental act.
Muttering of the five brahma-mantras (the 'five purifiers') and the Raudrī Gāyatrī; the last limb of the offering; mental for the Ratnaṭīkā.
Ash consecrated with the mantras, used for bathing thrice daily, lying on, re-bathing and initiation; the sign of the first stage.
The Atharvaśiras identifies all the elements with ash: 'fire is ash ... all this is ash'.
The ash of a cremation, smeared by a Kāpālika (Sattasaī) and listed by Yāmuna among the six Kāpāla insignia.
Bathing the body in consecrated ash at the three junctures of the day.
A further ash-bath after impurities such as eating, sneezing, spitting or evacuation, for purity and to show the sign; a secondary rule.
Flowers taken down from the image, worn to increase devotion and show the sign.
One who bears the Pāśupata sign (ash-bath, lying in ash etc.) that marks his stage, as other āśramas have their marks.
The temple (built by another) where the first-stage practitioner lives; the Ratnaṭīkā says it stands for the teacher.

notes: Homonym of the Buddhist technical term āyatana (sense-base).

definitions.definition: Being held in contempt by all beings, sought by the second-stage ascetic.
The contempt the ascetic courts; the wise one who is insulted becomes complete in austerity.
Dishonour, declared the highest of all restraints; Kauṇḍinya: it removes pride of birth and of householder status.
The second-stage ascetic who hides his Pāśupata sign while his conduct is manifest.
Conduct openly displayed while the sign is hidden.
Living unwashed, unshaven and ungroomed like a poor madman (the 'preta' of the sūtra being a living man), so that caste and āśrama marks are cut off.
Feigning sleep while awake, with a snoring sound in the throat.
Deliberately shaking the limbs as if struck by a wind-disorder.
Walking as if one's foot were injured.
Making signs of desire toward a young woman from a distance so as to be thought unchaste; the act is feigned and must not violate the restraints.
Acting as one who cannot tell pure from impure, fit from unfit (e.g. handling sticks and clods), without breaking the restraints.

notes: From the sūtra 'api tat kuryāt'; Ratnaṭīkā: apitatkaraṇa.

definitions.definition: Uttering meaningless, repetitive or self-contradictory words.
Keeping the vow, knowledge and pure words (mantras) concealed.
The madman's guise the ascetic adopts, wandering alone so that people call him mad and foolish.
The insulted wise ascetic, whose austerity is thereby complete.
The gift of oneself to the Lord, whose fruit is final non-return, as against ordinary gifts of cows, land and gold.
Performing the prescribed acts as the Lord's command; the supreme worship.
Enduring the three sufferings without remedy while keeping one's rule; the supreme austerity.
The Rudra-gāyatrī ('tatpuruṣāya vidmahe ...') muttered after impurity and as the chosen verse from which yoga proceeds.
An alternative verse to the Raudrī Gāyatrī for expiation and recitation (usually taken as the Aghora mantra).
Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa and Īśāna, one closing each adhyāya of the Sūtra; the Ratnaṭīkā calls them the five purifiers (pavitra).
The object of meditation, with fixation in the heart, in the third stage.
Holding the mind in the heart.
With the cave, the dwelling of the third stage.
The third gain, sought in the stage of conquest.
The dwelling of the fourth stage, not left until the body falls.
Setting of Kāpālika rites in literary portraits.
Livelihood of the first and third stages - whatever falls into the bowl.
Livelihood of the second stage: food cast away or given out of pity or curiosity.
Livelihood of the fourth stage: whatever comes unasked to one staying in the cremation ground.
The three livelihoods: alms, discarded food, and what is obtained.
Non-harming, celibacy, truthfulness, non-dealing and non-stealing (with the five niyamas also counted as yamas).
Non-anger, service of the teacher, purity, lightness of diet and vigilance.
Abstaining from worldly transactions; the fourth Pāśupata yama.
Attentiveness to what is to come, like guarding a sprout; a niyama, the fifth strength, and the state in which the end of suffering is reached.
Mental impurity whose absence (akaluṣamati) is the condition for yoga to arise; its removal is the first stage's purification.
The fruits of the means: knowledge, austerity, permanence (constant union with the god), steadiness and perfection.
What the practitioner strives to destroy: false knowledge, demerit, the cause of attachment, falling away and the root of the paśu-state.
Residence, observance, muttering-and-meditation, constant remembrance of Rudra, and grace.
The supports by whose power the practitioner grows: teacher, people, cave, cremation ground, Rudra.
The practitioner's fixed stations until the gain: manifest, unmanifest, conquest, cutting, completion.
The absolute removal of each impurity: of ignorance, demerit, what causes attachment, falling away, and the paśu-state.

Material (the threefold effect: disciple's and teacher's knowledge, the kalās such as darbha, ash, sandal, thread, flowers, incense, mantras, and the brahmin to be consecrated), time (forenoon), rite, image and teacher.
Devotion to the teacher, clarity of mind, conquest of opposites, merit and vigilance.

A technical term for the disciple's eight faculties of learning while living with the teacher (grasping, retaining, inferring, rejecting, understanding, speaking, service, right application); the first means.
The first stage, in which the Pāśupata sign is made manifest by ash-bathing and the rest; lived in the temple under the teacher.
The second stage, in which birth and sign are hidden and the ascetic courts dishonour among people.
The third stage, aimed at conquering the senses (and constant union with the god), in a cave or empty house.
The fourth stage, ending in the cutting [of bonds], in the cremation ground.
The fifth stage: complete cessation of all the practitioner's activity; its place is Rudra alone.
The first strength.
The third strength; endurance of heat and cold and the like, as cows and deer endure them.
The one who knows the nine groups and consecrates the disciple; a mere knower of texts without faith is a semblance of a teacher.
Consecration of a tested brahmin with mantra-sanctified ash before the southern image, with the hearing of the mantra.
The Pāśupata teachers of the line from Lakulīśa to Rāśīkara saluted daily; Jain doxographers list eighteen.
Name given by the Śaiva scriptures to the Pāśupata and Lākula (and skull-observing) division of Śaivism: knowledge 'beyond the states of the intellect', 'beyond the world'.
The other great division of Śaivism, beside the Atimārga, whose scriptures (Siddhānta and Bhairava tantras) describe and outrank the Atimārga.
The skull observance of the Lākulas (and Kāpālikas), 'beyond the world'; the Svacchanda calls the Atimārga knowledge lokātīta.

The skull-bearer's great vow: living with a skull-bowl and skull-staff in imitation of Bhairava's penance; its keepers are 'mahāvratins'. Yāmuna reports 'by taking the Kāpāla vow a man becomes an ascetic'.
The observance of the Lākula division (lokātīta), with skull and khaṭvāṅga.

notes: Homonym of the Vedic śrauta Mahāvrata rite, which is unrelated.

definitions.definition: The observance of those called kapālavratins, whom the Svacchanda places with the Pāśupatas beyond re-creation.
Name for skull-observing Śaiva ascetics; Guṇaratna counts the Mahāvratadharas as the third of four kinds of Śaiva ascetics, the Śiva Purāṇa honours them among Śaivas.
The human skull carried as begging-bowl; with the khaṭvāṅga a sub-insignia (upamudrā) of the Kāpālas (Yāmuna); eating from a skull is ascribed to the Kālāmukhas.
Staff crowned with a skull, a sub-insignia of the Kāpālas; its bell rings as Kapālakuṇḍalā flies.
Carried with the skull in the lokātīta observance.
A Śaiva ascetic keeping the skull vow; named with Kālāmukhas, Pāśupatas and Śaivas as one of four Māheśvara groups (Yāmuna; Vācaspati).
Śiva/Bhairava as bearer of Brahmā's skull; his 'excellent skull-bearer's guise' destroys the sin of those who remember it.
Name of the Kāpālika doctrine (Prabodhacandrodaya); the Kūrma Purāṇa lists 'Soma' among non-Vedic Śaiva scriptures.

notes: Etymology as 'Śiva with Umā (sa-umā)' is traditional/uncertain.

definitions.definition: Ear-ornament (or necklace), rucaka, earrings, crest-jewel, ash and sacred thread, with skull and khaṭvāṅga as sub-insignia; knowing and wearing them is said to bring release (Yāmuna's report).
Object of a meditation on the self, reported by Yāmuna as the Kāpāla means to nirvāṇa (restricted; opponent's report).
Human flesh as offering, in hostile literary portraits of Kāpālika and cremation-ground rites.
The sin incurred by Bhairava/Śiva in cutting off Brahmā's head, whose penance - wandering with the skull - the Kāpālika vow imitates.
The tīrtha (at Vārāṇasī in the Purāṇic story) where the skull fell from the Lord's hand and he was freed from brahmin-murder.
The deity of the Kāpālikas in hostile portraits (Mahābhairava worshipped with liquor and alleged human offerings); the skull-bearing form of Śiva.
Name of the Śaiva order known from Karnataka inscriptions; Yāmuna attributes skull and corpse-ash practices to it; Guṇaratna counts the Kālamukhas as the fourth kind of Śaiva ascetic.
The club held by Lakulīśa ('Lord with the club'), in the left hand in the Kāravaṇa-māhātmya's image.
Carrying a club is among the practices Yāmuna ascribes to the Kālāmukhas.
A rival account of liberation rejected by Rāmakaṇṭha: the transfer of [the Lord's qualities] into the perfected soul.

notes: Homonym of the Jyotiṣa term for the sun's entry into a sign.

definitions.definition: A rival account of liberation rejected by Rāmakaṇṭha: possession [of the soul by the Lord's qualities].
Among the siddha's powers: he 'enters all' and none can enter him (sarvāṃś cāviśati ... anāveśyaḥ).
A rival account of liberation rejected by Rāmakaṇṭha: the new production [of the Lord's qualities in the soul].
